title: Motion in a Plane — Chapter Summary
intro: This chapter promotes kinematics from one dimension to two. We introduce vectors as the language of two-dimensional motion, then apply that language to three classic problems: projectile motion, uniform circular motion, and relative velocity. The key idea is that 2D motion splits into two independent 1D problems linked only by time.

sections.heading: Scalars and vectors
bullets: A scalar is fully specified by a single number plus a unit (mass, temperature, speed, energy).
A vector needs BOTH magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force).
Vectors are drawn as arrows; length = magnitude, orientation = direction.
Two vectors are equal when both their magnitudes and directions agree — position on the page does not matter.
A unit vector has magnitude 1 and is used only to indicate direction (î, ĵ, k̂ along x, y, z).

sections.heading: Vector addition and resolution
bullets: Triangle law: place tail of B at head of A; resultant runs from tail of A to head of B.
Parallelogram law: complete the parallelogram on A and B; resultant is the diagonal from their common tail.
Magnitude of resultant: R² = A² + B² + 2 A B cos θ.
Direction of resultant from A: tan α = (B sin θ) / (A + B cos θ).
Resolution: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ — turns a 2D problem into two independent 1D problems.
Dot product A · B = A B cos θ is a scalar; cross product A × B has magnitude A B sin θ and is perpendicular to both.

sections.heading: Velocity and acceleration in 2D
bullets: If r(t) = x(t) î + y(t) ĵ then v = v_x î + v_y ĵ and a = a_x î + a_y ĵ.
The 1D kinematic equations apply component-wise when a is constant in magnitude AND direction.
Horizontal and vertical motions are independent — they share only the time t.
This decoupling is the central technique for every 2D constant-a problem.

sections.heading: Projectile motion
bullets: A projectile moves under gravity alone (air resistance neglected).
Initial components for launch speed u at angle θ: u_x = u cos θ (constant), u_y = u sin θ (decreasing under g).
Trajectory is a parabola: y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ).
Time of flight: T = 2 u sin θ / g.
Maximum height: H = u² sin² θ / (2 g).
Range on level ground: R = u² sin 2θ / g; maximised at θ = 45°.
Complementary launch angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range.

sections.heading: Uniform circular motion
bullets: Uniform = constant SPEED; the velocity still changes direction continuously.
Centripetal acceleration points toward the centre: a_c = v² / r = ω² r.
Angular speed ω = v / r; period T = 2π r / v = 2π / ω.
Centripetal force F = m v² / r is the NET inward force — not a new kind of force.
There is no outward 'centrifugal force' in the lab frame; the outward feeling is inertia.
Physical sources of F_c: tension (whirled stone), friction (turning car), gravity (orbiting satellite).

sections.heading: Relative velocity in 2D
bullets: Velocity of A as seen from B is v_AB = v_A − v_B (vector subtraction).
River-crossing for shortest PATH: boat heads partly upstream; sin θ = v_r / v_b. Possible only if v_b > v_r.
River-crossing for shortest TIME: boat heads straight across; river carries it downstream.
Aeroplane in a crosswind: pilot must crab into the wind so the side-component cancels.
General method: choose a frame, decompose vectors into components, recompose.

key_takeaways: Vectors carry magnitude AND direction; resolving them into components turns one 2D problem into two 1D problems.
In 2D motion with constant acceleration, the x- and y-components obey the 1D kinematic equations independently.
Projectile motion: trajectory is a parabola; T = 2 u sin θ / g, H = u² sin² θ / (2 g), R = u² sin 2θ / g; range maximum at θ = 45°.
Uniform circular motion has centripetal acceleration a_c = v² / r toward the centre; the required net inward force is F = m v² / r.
Relative velocity in 2D is a vector subtraction — used for river-crossing and crosswind problems.
Whatever the problem, the technique is the same: choose a frame, decompose, then recompose.

glossary.definition: A physical quantity that is fully specified by a single real number and a unit; it has magnitude but no direction. Examples: mass, time, temperature, energy.
A physical quantity that requires both magnitude and direction to be fully specified. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force.
A vector of magnitude exactly one, used purely to indicate direction. The standard Cartesian unit vectors are î, ĵ, k̂.
The process of expressing a vector as a sum of two perpendicular components along chosen axes, typically A_x = A cos θ and A_y = A sin θ.
A body thrown into space and subsequently moving under the influence of gravity alone (air resistance neglected).
The path traced by a moving particle. For an ideal projectile launched at an angle, the trajectory is a parabola.
The horizontal distance covered by a projectile from launch to its return to the launch height; R = u² sin 2θ / g on level ground.
Motion of a particle along a circle at constant speed; the velocity changes direction continuously even though its magnitude is constant.
The acceleration directed toward the centre of the circle in uniform circular motion, of magnitude a_c = v² / r = ω² r.
The net inward force required to keep a body in uniform circular motion: F = m v² / r. It is not a new kind of force — its physical origin can be tension, friction, gravity, etc.
The rate at which the angular position changes, ω = dθ/dt (radians per second); related to linear speed by v = ω r.
The velocity of one object as observed from another moving object: v_AB = v_A − v_B.
